case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an incarcerated person may recover damages under the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) against state prison officials in their individual capacities for substantially burdening the person’s religious exercise.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 2000cc-1(a) (RLUIPA institutionalized-persons provision), with remedial language in 42 U.S.C. § 2000cc-2(a) (authorizing “appropriate relief against a government”); related sovereign-immunity background under the Eleventh Amendment and Spending Clause enforcement principles.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Landor argues that RLUIPA’s guarantee of strict-scrutiny protection for incarcerated religious exercise is hollow if officials who violate it face no meaningful remedy. He contends that (1) RLUIPA’s authorization of “appropriate relief” should be read to include money damages against officials in their individual capacities (at least where equitable relief is unavailable or inadequate), (2) the Fifth Circuit’s contrary rule creates an accountability gap because injunctive relief is often moot (transfers, policy changes) and official-capacity damages are barred by sovereign immunity, and (3) recognizing individual-capacity damages is consistent with RLUIPA’s purpose and with how civil-rights statutes typically ensure enforcement—while not causing the feared “flood” of litigation, as experience under comparable strict-scrutiny regimes (e.g., RFRA in federal prisons) has not produced unmanageable case volume.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Louisiana maintains that RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages. In its view, RLUIPA was enacted primarily under the Spending Clause and conditions federal funds on state/local governmental conduct; such funding conditions must provide clear notice to the funding recipient, and nothing in RLUIPA clearly notifies states that individual employees will face personal monetary liability. Respondents also emphasize that the statute authorizes “appropriate relief against a government,” which they read as limited to governmental defendants (official-capacity suits) and equitable remedies, not damages against individuals. They further rely on the Supreme Court’s prior sovereign-immunity and Spending Clause cases to argue that damages are unavailable (at minimum against states and state officials in their official capacities) and warn that expanding liability would interfere with prison administration and invite burdensome litigation.
key_precedents: Pennhurst State School & Hospital v. Halderman (1981)

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains the analogy to Tanzin, but that case cannot do the work here because RLUIPA’s remedial clause is expressly limited to “appropriate relief against a government,” which is a meaningful textual narrowing absent from RFRA. Justice Kagan’s point about Pennhurst is decisive for me: in a Spending Clause bargain, Congress must provide unmistakably clear notice before acceptance of funds can be said to expose anyone—especially individual employees—to personal-capacity monetary liability, and this statute does not. Sossamon reinforces that this very remedial language is not a clear statement for damages in the RLUIPA context, making it even less plausible to infer a broader personal-capacity damages remedy. A minimalist holding—RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages—respects the text, our Spending Clause clear-notice precedents, and institutional legitimacy without foreclosing Congress from speaking more clearly.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the analogy to Tanzin, but that case involved RFRA’s materially different remedial structure and did not contain RLUIPA’s limitation to “appropriate relief against a government.” As Justice Kagan emphasizes, the ordinary public meaning of “against a government” points to entity or official-capacity relief, not personal-capacity damages, and reading it otherwise would treat the limiting words as surplusage. Chief Justice Roberts’s Pennhurst point independently forecloses petitioner’s theory: in a Spending Clause bargain Congress must give unmistakable notice of any personal monetary exposure, and RLUIPA’s text does not clearly warn States (or their employees) of individual-capacity damages. Sossamon’s insistence that this same language is not a clear statement for monetary liability in this context reinforces that we should not extend Tanzin by implication.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the analogy to Tanzin, which read “appropriate relief” to include damages, and Justice Sotomayor is right to note the practical remedial gap if damages are unavailable. But Justice Kagan’s emphasis on the limiting words “against a government” is decisive under a textualist reading: that phrase naturally points to entity/official-capacity relief, not personal-capacity suits. Layered on top, as the Chief Justice stresses, Pennhurst’s clear-notice rule in a Spending Clause statute makes it implausible to infer individual monetary exposure for state employees from equivocal language—especially when Sossamon already found this very remedial formulation insufficiently clear for damages. Given those textual and structural constraints, any expansion to personal-capacity damages should come from Congress, not this Court.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains Tanzin v. Tanvir’s reading of “appropriate relief” to include individual-capacity damages, particularly where injunctive relief can become moot for incarcerated plaintiffs. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief emphasize, RLUIPA’s remedial clause is textually narrower—authorizing relief only “against a government”—and, as a Spending Clause statute, it triggers Pennhurst’s unmistakable-clear-notice requirement before we infer any monetary-liability regime tied to accepting federal funds. Sossamon’s conclusion that this same language is not a clear statement for damages in the RLUIPA/Spending Clause context undercuts petitioner’s attempt to leverage Tanzin beyond RFRA’s different structure. The remedial gap is real and troubling in practice, but under my approach it cannot substitute for the clear congressional authorization needed to expose state employees to personal damages via a funding-condition bargain.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Tanzin analogy: “appropriate relief” can include damages against officers. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, RLUIPA’s remedial clause is textually narrowed to relief “against a government,” and that limiting phrase is hard to square with personal-capacity liability as a matter of ordinary meaning and statutory coherence. Justice Barrett’s Pennhurst point is decisive under a pragmatic textualist lens: in a Spending Clause bargain, Congress must give unmistakable notice if acceptance of funds will expose individuals to personal damages, and RLUIPA’s government-directed phrasing does not do that. Sossamon, while arising in the sovereign-immunity posture, reinforces that this very remedial language is not a clear damages authorization in this statutory setting, making Tanzin’s RFRA-based reading a poor fit here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains Tanzin v. Tanvir’s recognition that “appropriate relief” can encompass damages, but that inference cannot survive RLUIPA’s express limitation to relief “against a government.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, RLUIPA is a Spending Clause bargain, so Pennhurst requires unmistakably clear notice before we treat acceptance of funds as consenting to a personal-capacity damages regime for state employees; this text does not provide it. Justice Barrett’s focus on ordinary public meaning reinforces that “against a government” naturally targets the entity/official-capacity relief, not individual liability, and Sossamon’s treatment of this same remedial language confirms it lacks the requisite clarity for monetary exposure in this statutory setting. Whatever the policy concern about remedial gaps, our job is to read the enacted words within their constitutional structure, not to supply remedies Congress did not clearly authorize.

In a Spending Clause statute, Pennhurst’s clear-notice rule does real work: States must have unmistakable notice of the liabilities attached to accepting funds, and nothing in RLUIPA clearly signals that state employees would face personal monetary exposure. RLUIPA’s remedial clause is not just “appropriate relief”; it is “appropriate relief against a government,” which, as the Chief Justice notes, naturally reads as entity/official-capacity relief and does not clearly alert States (or their employees) to personal damages exposure. John Roberts.reasoning: RLUIPA’s remedial provision authorizes only “appropriate relief against a government,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000cc-2(a), and in the Spending Clause context we require clear notice to the funding recipient before imposing monetary liability, see Pennhurst State School & Hospital v. Halderman (1981). In Sossamon v. Texas (2011), we held that this same remedial language does not clearly authorize damages against a State, reflecting the statute’s insufficient clarity as to monetary remedies, and that logic counsels against extending RLUIPA to personal-capacity damages absent unmistakable congressional authorization. Tanzin v. Tanvir (2020) construed identical words in RFRA to permit individual-capacity damages, but RFRA is not Spending Clause legislation and does not raise the same clear-notice concerns for States and their officials. To preserve institutional legitimacy and adhere to precedent and federalism principles, I would not read RLUIPA to create individual-capacity damages without a clearer statement from Congress.

Because RLUIPA operates as Spending Clause legislation conditioning federal funds, Pennhurst requires Congress to speak with clear notice if it means to expose individuals to personal monetary liability, and this statute does not clearly do so. Samuel Alito.reasoning: RLUIPA authorizes “appropriate relief against a government,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000cc-2(a), and that text naturally targets governmental defendants, not individual employees in their personal capacities. Because RLUIPA rests largely on the Spending Clause, any condition exposing individuals to personal monetary liability must be stated with unmistakable clarity; under Pennhurst and Sossamon, Congress did not provide clear notice that acceptance of federal funds would subject state officers to individual-capacity damages. case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes an incarcerated person to obtain money damages against state prison officials (in their individual capacities) for substantially burdening the person’s religious exercise.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act of 2000 (RLUIPA), 42 U.S.C. §§ 2000cc et seq., especially § 2000cc-2(a) (creating a private cause of action and authorizing “appropriate relief against a government”), and the related remedial/sovereign-immunity framework under the Eleventh Amendment and Spending Clause enforcement principles.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Landor argues that RLUIPA’s express cause of action allowing “appropriate relief against a government” should be read to include damages against responsible prison officials at least in their individual capacities; otherwise, RLUIPA frequently provides no meaningful remedy because many violations are completed harms that cannot be fully cured by prospective injunctive relief. He emphasizes that RLUIPA imposes a strict-scrutiny standard on prison burdens of religious exercise and that limiting relief to injunctions undermines Congress’s remedial design and deterrence goals. Supporting amici contend (1) robust remedies are historically associated with religious-liberty protections, (2) damages are often the only realistic way to redress past burdens on religious exercise, and (3) allowing damages would not create an unmanageable flood of litigation, pointing to the federal prison experience under RFRA (strict scrutiny with damages) as evidence that prisons can function under that regime.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Louisiana and its corrections officials contend that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize money damages against state actors, particularly given the statute’s phrasing (“appropriate relief against a government”), the sovereign-immunity backdrop, and the Court’s insistence that Congress speak clearly when exposing states or state-related defendants to damages liability. They rely on existing Supreme Court interpretations that have already foreclosed damages against states under RLUIPA and argue that extending RLUIPA to individual-capacity damages would be inconsistent with RLUIPA’s Spending Clause character (i.e., the statute operates like a funding contract with states, which cannot fairly be read to impose personal damages liability on individual employees absent unmistakably clear notice). They also stress administrability and institutional-security concerns—arguing prisons need operational flexibility and that expanding damages remedies could chill legitimate correctional decisionmaking and increase burdensome litigation.
key_precedents: City of Boerne v. Flores, 521 U.S. 507 (1997)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that Tanzin treated similar language as reaching traditional damages and that injunction-only relief can be inadequate for completed harms, particularly in prisons. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, RLUIPA’s cause of action is framed as “appropriate relief against a government,” and in a Spending Clause statute Pennhurst demands unmistakably clear notice before we read the funding “contract” to authorize a significant monetary remedy—especially personal-capacity damages against individuals who are not “a government.” Sossamon, while driven by sovereign-immunity concerns, is still highly probative on the key interpretive point: Congress did not speak clearly enough in this statute to make money damages the default “appropriate relief,” and it would be anomalous to infer broader personal liability where even state-entity damages are not clearly authorized. Under a minimalist, precedent-respecting approach, the narrower course is to hold that RLUIPA permits equitable relief (including official-capacity injunctions) but does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that, as in Tanzin, damages are often the ordinary remedy needed to redress completed violations, and injunctive relief may be practically inadequate in prisons. But under the text Congress enacted—"appropriate relief against a government"—I agree with Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan that the object of relief is the government, not individual employees in their personal capacities, and that mismatch is decisive for a textualist. In this Spending Clause context, Pennhurst’s clear-notice rule reinforces that we should not infer a significant, non-obvious condition (personal damages exposure for officers) from ambiguous language, and Sossamon’s insistence that the same phrase lacks the requisite clarity about damages in RLUIPA further confirms the point rather than distinguishing it away. Tanzin’s reading of RFRA does not undermine this conclusion because RFRA is not a funding “contract” with States and thus does not carry the same clear-statement baseline.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Sossamon addressed sovereign immunity rather than personal-capacity liability and that Tanzin treated similar language as allowing damages, but that analogy still fails in the Spending Clause context where Pennhurst demands unmistakably clear notice of the liability regime attached to the State’s acceptance of funds. As Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the statute authorizes “appropriate relief against a government,” which is a poor textual fit for imposing personal-capacity damages on individuals who are not themselves “a government,” and it would be anomalous to infer broader individual damages where the same phrase was insufficiently clear to expose the State to damages. Sossamon’s insistence on clarity in this very statutory setting reinforces that “appropriate relief” is not a clear damages authorization, and I do not think we can supply that missing clarity by appealing to remedial desirability in prison litigation. Whatever the policy case for damages, Congress can say so expressly, and under our clear-statement rules we should not extend RLUIPA beyond equitable/official-capacity relief on this text.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Pennhurst point is the most serious: Spending Clause statutes must give States clear notice of the conditions they accept. But that clear-notice rule is about the State’s bargain and its exposure, and it does not persuasively explain why Congress’s authorization of “appropriate relief” for a proven statutory violation must be read to exclude the traditional damages remedy against the actual violator when the State itself may remain shielded by sovereign immunity (as in Sossamon). Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch stress that the text says relief “against a government,” yet RLUIPA’s definition of “government” includes “officials” and “other person[s] acting under color of State law,” making it textually plausible that Congress contemplated suits reaching individuals, and “appropriate relief” ordinarily includes damages for completed injuries unless clearly displaced. Given the prison context (Cutter/Holt) and the practical reality that injunction-only relief often leaves past burdens on religious exercise without meaningful redress or deterrence, I cannot infer that Congress silently chose that remedial gap absent a clearer exclusion.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that Tanzin reflects a strong background presumption that “appropriate relief” includes damages and that injunction-only relief can be practically hollow for past harms, especially in prisons. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, RLUIPA’s Spending Clause posture triggers Pennhurst’s clear-notice rule, and the text authorizes relief only “against a government,” which is an awkward—and to my mind insufficiently clear—hook for imposing personal-capacity damages on individual employees who are not “a government.” Sossamon, though framed in sovereign-immunity terms, reinforces that this very phrase is not a clear statement for money damages in this statutory setting; it would be anomalous to infer broader individual damages liability where Congress did not clearly authorize damages even as to the governmental defendant. On a pragmatic textualist reading, the more coherent, workable interpretation is equitable relief against governmental/official-capacity defendants, leaving any expansion to damages to Congress’s clearer drafting.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that, as in Tanzin, damages are often the only meaningful remedy for completed violations, and limiting relief to injunctions can leave plaintiffs empty-handed. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief note, RLUIPA’s text authorizes “appropriate relief against a government,” which is a poor linguistic fit for personal-capacity damages against individuals who are not themselves “a government,” especially in a Spending Clause regime where Pennhurst demands clear notice of liability consequences tied to funding. Sossamon matters here not merely for sovereign immunity but because it confirms that this very phrase is not an unmistakably clear authorization of damages in this statutory setting; it would be anomalous to read the same words to impose potentially significant personal damages liability when they do not clearly impose damages liability on the governmental recipient. Tanzin is distinguishable because RFRA expressly reaches “officials” and does not operate as a federal-funds “contract,” so its remedial presumption cannot supply the clarity Congress did not provide in RLUIPA.

But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, RLUIPA is Spending Clause legislation, so Pennhurst requires unmistakably clear notice of the liabilities attached to accepting federal funds; the phrase “appropriate relief against a government” does not clearly authorize personal-capacity money damages against individuals who are not “a government.” Sossamon, while framed through sovereign immunity, reinforces that this exact statutory language is not a clear statement for damages in this context, and it would be anomalous to infer broader personal liability for employees when the statute does not clearly impose damages liability on the governmental funding recipient. Under my institutionalist approach, expanding damages in prison litigation absent a clear congressional instruction is a significant remedial move better left to Congress, so Tanzin does not undermine the Spending Clause notice analysis here.

But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, RLUIPA is Spending Clause legislation, so Pennhurst’s clear-notice rule is part of the interpretive baseline; “appropriate relief against a government” does not speak unmistakably to imposing personal-capacity damages on individual employees who are not “a government.” Sossamon, though framed in sovereign-immunity terms, reinforces that this exact phrase is not a clear statement for money damages in this statutory setting, making it textually and doctrinally difficult to infer a different, broader damages remedy against individuals. Policy concerns about deterrence cannot supply the clear statement Congress did not provide, so I remain with the Respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Tanzin analogy and her remedial-concerns point are the hardest to answer, because damages are often the only meaningful remedy for completed burdens on incarcerated people’s religious exercise. But in this Spending Clause context, Pennhurst’s clear-notice rule alters the baseline: it is not procedurally fair or administrable to treat a State’s acceptance of funds as implicitly authorizing personal-capacity damages exposure for individual employees when the statute authorizes only “appropriate relief against a government.” As Justice Kagan underscores, it would be anomalous to infer silent individual damages liability where Sossamon already indicates the same language does not unmistakably authorize damages against the State itself in this statutory setting. Given that the text targets governmental defendants and Congress can speak clearly when it wants damages, I do not think Sotomayor’s reading overcomes the clear-statement constraints that govern RLUIPA.

John Roberts.reasoning: RLUIPA’s remedial clause authorizes “appropriate relief against a government,” 42 U.S.C. § 2000cc-2(a), but Sossamon v. Texas held that this language is not a clear statement sufficient to expose States to damages, reflecting the Court’s insistence on unmistakable notice in this Spending Clause setting. Tanvir does not compel a different result because it construed RFRA outside the same sovereign-immunity/Spending Clause notice constraints that drove Sossamon’s reading of identical language in RLUIPA.
